headline: HEIC decode works fully offline from file:// in a blob-URL worker — a genuine 11.94 MP HEVC HEIC decodes in ~950 ms with zero network requests — but the decode pattern in the libheif-js README leaks 6.35 MB of wasm heap per image (~3.2 GB projected at the PRD's 500 photos), and the two-line fix is undocumented.

findings.capability: libheif-wasm/libheif-bundle.js loads as a CLASSIC <script> and initialises with zero network requests
findings.file_url: works — cold init 45.0 ms median over 5 fresh browser processes (script parse 22.7 ms + libheif() factory 22.3 ms); exactly 2 requests total (the HTML + the bundle .js), 0 for *.wasm, 0 remote, 0 fetch/XHR/WebSocket/EventSource tripwire hits
findings.http_url: works — identical: 2 requests, 0 wasm, 0 remote, 0 tripwire hits; cold init 53.4 ms
findings.detail: The global exposed by the script tag is an Emscripten MODULARIZE FACTORY, not the module — you must call libheif() before new .HeifDecoder(). The README's `new libheif.HeifDecoder()` fails in the browser with 'not a constructor'. Static corroboration that no wasm fetch is possible: the bundle embeds a 1,379,076-char base64 literal decoding to 1,034,307 bytes vs the standalone libheif.wasm on disk at 1,034,305 bytes, and contains no instantiateStreaming call.

findings.capability: Decode a genuine 12 MP HEVC-coded HEIC to RGBA and write it out as a PNG
findings.file_url: works — 3992x2992 (11.94 MP), 994 ms median steady-state, 1180 ms first-decode (JIT warm-up); 47,776,256-byte RGBA; PNG written (22.6 MB) and visually verified as a correct aerial coastline photo
findings.http_url: works — byte-identical pixels (sampled channel sum 1282876 matches file:// exactly), 1378 ms
findings.detail: Fixture is a real HEVC-in-HEIF: ftyp heic/mif1 with a `grid` derived image over 48 hvc1 tiles and 50 infe entries — the tiled layout an iPhone writes. NOT an AVIF stand-in; no AVIF fallback was needed and none was used. No npm packages were installed (sharp was never required). Decode cost is linear in megapixels across a 13x size range: 83.2 ms/MP.

findings.capability: Pure asm.js build (libheif/libheif.js) as the alternative
findings.file_url: works — cold init 115.2 ms; 12 MP decode 1,997 ms median (167.2 ms/MP); zero network; identical pixels
findings.http_url: works — cold init 118.2 ms; 12 MP decode 2,499 ms
findings.detail: Uniformly 2.01x slower than the wasm bundle at every image size tested (1.94x-2.52x), from a file that is 42% LARGER (2.08 MB vs 1.46 MB). It has no advantage on this target. Recommendation: ship the wasm bundle.

findings.capability: Blob-URL Web Worker + importScripts(ABSOLUTE url of the bundle) — PRD 7.9 worker-threaded decode
findings.file_url: works — this is the key result. Worker init 93.5 ms, 12 MP decode 1,594 ms (first, incl. warm-up). importScripts of an absolute file:// URL from inside a blob worker succeeds even though the page origin is 'null'
findings.detail: Build the URL with new URL(rel, location.href).href. Playwright routing does NOT surface blob-worker subresource loads, so the no-network claim for the worker rests on the in-worker fetch tripwire (0 hits), the base64-embedding evidence, and the inlined-source variant below.

findings.file_url: blocked: "Failed to execute 'importScripts' on 'WorkerGlobalScope': The URL '../../../../node_modules/libheif-js/libheif-wasm/libheif-bundle.js' is invalid."
findings.detail: A relative path resolves against the blob: URL base and is rejected outright. The absolute URL is mandatory, not a stylistic choice.

findings.capability: Classic (non-blob) Web Worker from a sibling .js file — the obvious way to ship a worker
findings.file_url: blocked: "Failed to construct 'Worker': Script at 'file:///.../worker_classic.js' cannot be accessed from origin 'null'." Throws at the constructor.
findings.detail: This is the trap for PRD section 8's local-HTML delivery. Any design that ships worker.js next to index.html works in dev over localhost and breaks the instant the user double-clicks the HTML file. The blob-URL worker is the only portable option.

findings.capability: Blob-URL worker with the whole bundle SOURCE inlined in the HTML (<script type="text/plain"> -> .textContent -> Blob), no importScripts at all
findings.file_url: works — 1 network request in the entire session (the HTML itself). Fastest init measured: factory 23.5 ms, decode 1,318 ms
findings.detail: The true zero-external-request fallback if a single-file deliverable is ever wanted. Cost: a 1.47 MB HTML file. Proves conclusively that no fetch is involved anywhere in decode.

findings.capability: Transfer the decoded RGBA buffer out of the worker (zero-copy)
findings.file_url: works — 47,776,256-byte ArrayBuffer transferred via postMessage(..., [buf]); received with byteLength preserved and instanceof ArrayBuffer true
findings.detail: The buffer IS transferable. Transfer it; structured-cloning 48 MB per image would be a significant unnecessary cost at 500 photos.

findings.capability: OffscreenCanvas derivative generation inside the worker (PRD 7.9 previews/thumbs, PRD 8 sidecars)
findings.file_url: works — full ingest step per image (1 worker, median): decode 1,033 ms + 1600px preview JPEG 41 ms + 320px thumb JPEG 2.8 ms + full-size JPEG sidecar 199 ms = 1,430 ms total
findings.http_url: n/a (not re-run; no reason to differ — the page-level canvas path was verified identical under both)
findings.detail: convertToBlob works in a blob worker under file://. HEIC decode is 81% of the whole per-image pipeline, so optimisation effort belongs nowhere else. Derivative sizes: sidecar 3,323,667 B (11% LARGER than the 2,994,394 B HEIC it came from — 1.66 GB per 500 photos), 1600px preview 548,364 B, 320px thumb 25,425 B.

findings.file_url: measured — 1w: 1,266 ms/img (0.79 img/s); 2w: 728 ms/img (1.37 img/s); 4w: 446 ms/img (2.24 img/s, 2.84x); 8w: 457 ms/img (2.19 img/s, 2.83x)
findings.detail: Scaling stops dead at the core count — 8 workers is measurably no better than 4 and doubles memory. Size the pool at navigator.hardwareConcurrency, capped; do not oversubscribe.

findings.capability: Wasm heap stability across a 500-photo-scale run — THE BLOCKER
findings.file_url: BROKEN with the documented pattern, FIXED with the correct one. new HeifDecoder() per image: heap grows 72 MB -> 446 MB over 60 decodes, 6.35 MB/decode, still climbing (74 MB over the last 20) -> ~3,245 MB projected at 500. ONE shared HeifDecoder + image.free() on every returned handle: heap dead flat at 72 MB across 200 sequential 12 MP decodes, zero growth, identical pixel checksums (5,105,342) at decode 1 and 200, median 953 ms
findings.http_url: n/a (memory behaviour is transport-independent; measured under file:// only)
findings.detail: Root cause read out of the shipped wrapper: HeifDecoder.prototype.decode frees its heif_context only on the NEXT decode() call on the SAME instance, and there is no destructor. A fresh decoder per image strands one full context (file bytes + decoded planes) forever; Emscripten heaps only grow. Four variants tested at 60 decodes: new-decoder-alone, new-decoder+free(), and shared-decoder-alone ALL leak 6.35 MB/decode identically. Only shared-decoder AND free() together is flat. Both halves required; neither alone helps at all. Invisible at the 2-3 image scale anyone tests by hand.

findings.capability: Signalling unsupported / corrupt files (PRD 7.9 'flag unsupported files at load')
findings.file_url: partially works — decode() NEVER throws. JPEG input -> [] (len 0); 4 KB of 0x41 -> []; empty buffer -> []. But a truncated HEIC (first 50 KB of a 2.9 MB file) -> returns 1 image reporting a full, valid-looking 3992x2992
findings.detail: Treat decode() returning length 0 as 'unsupported'. The truncation case is the trap: metadata parses, a handle is returned, dimensions look right, and the failure only surfaces when image.display() invokes its callback with null. Ingest error detection must hang off the display() callback, not off decode().

architectural_implications: The ingest worker MUST create exactly ONE HeifDecoder and reuse it for every image, AND call .free() on every handle in the array returned by decode() — not just images[0], since multi-image HEICs (thumbnail pairs, Live Photos) return several. Both are required; either alone leaks 6.35 MB/image and reaches ~3.2 GB at 500 photos, killing the tab. Add this as a row in PRD section 8's constraint table or the mitigation will be lost.

The app MUST ship libheif-js/libheif-wasm/libheif-bundle.js (1.46 MB, wasm inlined as base64) and MUST NOT ship libheif-wasm/libheif.js (81 KB + separate 1.03 MB .wasm), because the latter fetches its .wasm at runtime — impossible from a file:// page. The asm.js build is 2.01x slower from a larger file and has no advantage on a Chromium-only target.

Decode workers MUST be blob-URL workers, not classic worker files. new Worker('./worker.js') throws at construction under file:// ('cannot be accessed from origin null'), so the obvious approach works over localhost in dev and breaks the moment a user double-clicks the HTML — exactly PRD section 8's delivery model.

Inside the worker, importScripts MUST be given an ABSOLUTE URL built with new URL(rel, location.href).href. A relative path resolves against the blob: base and throws 'The URL is invalid' under both file:// and http://.

The worker pool size MUST be capped at navigator.hardwareConcurrency. Measured scaling stops dead at the core count: 8 workers gave 2.19 img/s vs 4 workers' 2.24 img/s while doubling memory (each worker holds its own ~72 MB wasm arena).
The decoded RGBA ArrayBuffer MUST be transferred, not cloned, when leaving the worker — 47.8 MB per 12 MP image, verified transferable and received intact.

Ingest failure detection MUST hang off the image.display() callback receiving null, NOT off decode(). decode() never throws; a truncated HEIC returns a handle reporting full valid dimensions. Only a decode() return of length 0 reliably means 'unsupported format'.

PRD section 8's HEIC sidecar decision needs a size warning in the UI: a full-size q0.90 JPEG sidecar is 3,323,667 bytes against the 2,994,394-byte HEIC it came from — 11% LARGER, or +1.66 GB for a 500-photo set, roughly doubling the source folder. Consider generating the 1600px preview (548 KB) for display and deferring the full sidecar to export time.

PRD section 11 phase 1 can proceed. Budget ~4 minutes (241 s) of one-time ingest for 500 x 12 MP HEICs on 4 cores including previews, thumbnails and sidecars, on a modest 2.1 GHz Xeon VM — a modern laptop will be faster. This validates the 'one-time, cached, worker-threaded, resumable' mitigation as written.
Budget one throwaway warm-up decode per worker: the first decode in a fresh context is ~20% slower (1,180 ms vs 994 ms) from JIT warm-up.
The libheif global from a <script> tag is a factory function, not the module. Call libheif() first — the README's browser example is wrong and fails with 'HeifDecoder is not a constructor'.
unverified: Real iPhone provenance of the 12 MP fixture. It is structurally an iPhone-style HEIC (grid derived image over 48 hvc1 tiles at 3992x2992, 2 Exif boxes) but carries no Apple maker-note, so I cannot claim it came off an iPhone. It IS unambiguously genuine HEVC-in-HEIF, not AVIF.
10-bit / HDR HEIC, Live Photos, depth maps and burst containers. All three fixtures were 8-bit stills.
EXIF orientation handling (irot/imir boxes). Untested and a plausible source of sideways thumbnails in the grid — worth a follow-up probe since PRD 7.9 generates thumbnails at ingest.
Headed Chromium on real hardware. Everything was headless Chromium on a 4 vCPU Xeon @ 2.10 GHz cloud VM. Absolute times will differ; the 2.01x wasm/asm ratio and the memory behaviour should not.

The File System Access API path. Bytes were handed to the page via page.evaluate — equivalent to a File.arrayBuffer() result — but the actual directory-handle -> getFile() -> decode chain was not exercised. That belongs to the ingest probe.
Sidecar disk writes and IndexedDB persistence/quota behaviour. Out of scope here; only artefact sizes were measured.

Playwright routing did not surface the blob worker's importScripts of a file:// URL, so the worker's zero-network claim rests on the in-worker fetch/XHR tripwire (0 hits), the base64-embedding evidence, and the inlined-source variant that makes exactly 1 request in the whole session. Page-level file:// requests WERE observed by routing, so routing does see file:// traffic in general.
Sustained behaviour past 200 sequential decodes in one worker. Flat at 200; not run to the full 500.

Whether http:// parity holds for the OffscreenCanvas derivative pipeline and parallel worker scaling — both were run under file:// only. The page-level canvas path was verified identical under both transports, so divergence is unlikely.
Memory behaviour under http:// was not separately measured; it is transport-independent by construction.
